title: Meta-research on transparency shares its own data more often
text:
ImportantThis result is exploratory, not confirmatory



It was run against a one-page proposal rather than a full protocol, and it has not been reviewed by anyone. Three things follow and none of them are repairable after the fact:

The grading rule was developed on the analysis data. Statements were read to design it. Reading was blind to the exposure, which limits the damage, but a rule that has seen the data it will be applied to is not a pre-specified instrument.
Three of four sensitivity analyses are post hoc, two of them invented in response to defects found during the run.
Hand validation has not been done, so the rule’s agreement with a person is unknown.

The one property that does hold is the important one: the protocol was published and timestamped in git before the analysis ran, so the question could not be redefined after the answer was known. That makes this a real finding worth following up. It does not make it a confirmatory test, and it should not be cited as one.
A full protocol is at P01-v2, written after this run, which is why any result under it has to come from data this analysis did not use.
Analysis run by Claude Opus 5 on 2026-09-16. Code at studies/P01-advocacy-and-practice/.

title: Meta-research on transparency shares its own data more often
section: Two defects found during the run, and what each cost
text:
Two defects found during the run, and what each cost
Both were found by checking the result rather than by the code failing. Neither raised an error, and the first produced a plausible answer that was partly an artifact.

The extractor read papers’ own results as their statements
A meta-research paper about data availability contains sections called “Data availability over time” and “Extraction of data availability status” in its own methods and results. The first extractor walked the whole article, found those, and graded the paper actionable because such sections are full of repository URLs. Four of the 43 exposed records were contaminated, and the signature was visible from outside: the exposed arm hit the fuzzy title-matching routes three times more often than the unexposed arm.
A publisher-assigned sec-type="data-availability" does not protect against this. One article carries that attribute on a numbered methods section. Location does protect against it: a data availability statement is front or back matter, and a numbered section of the narrative is the paper’s argument rather than its disclosure. Extraction is now restricted to <front> and <back>.
The repair was not purely subtractive. One article’s real statement sits in <front> and was being shadowed by its own results section.
Cost: the uncorrected odds ratio was 3.86. After the fix it is higher, not lower. The artifact was not what was producing the effect, which is not what was expected when the check began.


The grading rule downgraded deposits that also offered data on request
The rule tested for an on-request clause before testing for a repository, on the reasoning that “available from the corresponding author at an email address” contains something that looks like a locator and is a refusal. That is right for a bare URL and wrong for a named repository. One article deposits its code on GitHub and OSF and separately says the raw Scopus data cannot be released under license; it shared what it could, and the rule called it declarative.
A named repository now outranks a co-occurring on-request clause. Six of 574 statements carry both, five of them a named repository.
Cost: all six are in the unexposed arm, so the correction raises the comparison rate and works against the hypothesis. The odds ratio fell from 4.67 to 4.40.

section: The author’s own papers are in this corpus
text:
The author’s own papers are in this corpus
A tier A search for meta-research retrieves the work of anyone who does meta-research, including whoever is running the study. Two articles in the analysis set name the author’s own repositories. Both are in the exposed arm and both are graded actionable, so their presence pushes the estimate in the direction of the hypothesis. Removing them changes the odds ratio from 4.40 to 4.10. Reported rather than silently dropped.

title: Meta-research on transparency shares its own data more often
text:
What this does not show

It is not causal and the design cannot make it so. A researcher who studies data sharing and a researcher who shares data may simply be the same kind of person, or may work in the same few journals with the same few policies. The journal random intercept absorbs the average journal but not an interaction between a journal’s policy and a paper’s topic.
43 exposed records is thin. The smallest effect this design could have detected at 80 percent power was a rise from 20.5 to 48.9 percent. The observed effect is larger than that floor, which is why it is visible; an effect half this size would have been missed, and a null here would have ruled out very little.
The exposure is a vocabulary match, not a judgment. A paper labelled as a transparency topic may mention data sharing once in passing. That misclassification is non-differential with respect to the outcome and biases toward the null, so it weakens this finding rather than manufacturing it.
60 percent PMC coverage is not random. 742 corpus records have no PMCID and 89 more are in PMC as metadata only. Open-access availability is itself correlated with transparency practice, so the sample leans transparent. This is stated in the protocol and is not fixable within the design.
The grading rule has been validated by a model and not yet by a person. See below.

title: Meta-research on transparency shares its own data more often
text:
Validation still outstanding
The protocol calls for 100 statements graded by hand to measure where the rule disagrees. studies/P01-advocacy-and-practice/out/validation-sample.csv holds that sample with an empty hand_grade column, and the agreement will be reported here when it is filled in.
What has happened instead is weaker and is labeled as such: 40 statements were read and graded by the same model that wrote the rule, which found the second defect above. A model checking its own rule is not an independent check, and the kappa against a person is not yet known.

title: Do meta-research studies follow the guidelines they audit others by?
text:
ImportantStatus: design. Frame counted. The scoring instrument is the obstacle. Not a protocol.



The frame is large: 630 tier A records and 685 frame records declare a cross-sectional or methodological design, of which 67 and 197 respectively name a reporting guideline.
What blocks this from being a protocol is not data but measurement: scoring adherence to STROBE means reading 22 items per article, and no validated automatic scorer exists. Section 5 is honest that this is the most expensive study of the set per unit of evidence.

title: Do meta-research studies follow the guidelines they audit others by?
text:
1. The question
Meta-research grades other people’s papers against reporting checklists. Most meta-research is itself a cross-sectional study of a sample of articles, and cross-sectional studies have a checklist: STROBE. A field that measures adherence and does not meet it is making an argument against its own instrument.

title: Do meta-research studies follow the guidelines they audit others by?
text:
2. Hypothesis
Meta-research articles that themselves assess guideline adherence report their own methods more completely than meta-research articles that do not.
The hypothesis is deliberately internal rather than a comparison against non-meta-research, because a comparison across fields would confound topic with venue with design. This is the same structure as P01v2, and the same criticism applies to it.
Primary null. Adherence does not differ by whether the article’s own subject is reporting quality.
What would falsify it. No difference, or worse adherence among the auditors.

title: Do meta-research studies follow the guidelines they audit others by?
section: 5. Outcome, and why this is expensive
text:
5. Outcome, and why this is expensive
A STROBE-based adherence score over the items that apply to a study of documents rather than of people. Not all 22 items apply; the applicable subset is fixed in advance and published with the protocol, because choosing which items apply after scoring is how an adherence study manufactures its own result.
Scoring requires reading. The realistic options are:

The author scores a random sample of 150 articles. Precise, and the ceiling on sample size.
Models score all of them after being validated against the author’s 150, gated at kappa 0.70 per item group, with items that fail the gate dropped and reported as dropped.

Option 2 is the design, with option 1 as its reference standard, and neither can start until the author’s 150 exist.

title: Do meta-research conclusions soften between preprint and journal?
text:
ImportantStatus: reduced protocol, by the decision rule this document wrote before the number was known.



Both linkage probes have run. 66 of 1790 tier A records and 75 of 7572 frame records have a preprint version: 141 pairs, a rate of 3.7 and 1.0 percent respectively.
Section 4 stated, before either number was known, that 200 or more pairs makes this a full protocol, 80 to 200 makes it a reduced one with a single binary outcome and no subgroup analyses, and under 80 makes it an agenda item. 141 falls in the middle band, so the reduced form is what this document now specifies. The rule is applied as written rather than renegotiated, which is the only thing that made writing it in advance worth doing.
Restricting to biomedical preprint servers, excluding arXiv and SSRN, leaves 108 pairs, which is still inside the 80 to 200 band. The biomedical restriction is therefore the primary analysis, not a subgroup, because this project is about biomedical meta-research and a result carried by arXiv preprints would not be about that.
A first draft of this section asserted that 108 was “below the 80 the rule requires” and used that to justify keeping arXiv in the primary analysis. 108 is not below 80. The claim contradicted the number printed two sentences above it, and it is recorded here rather than silently corrected because it is the third time in this project that a sentence reasoning about a computed value came out backwards.

title: Do meta-research conclusions soften between preprint and journal?
text:
1. The question
Meta-research criticizes the literature, and peer reviewers are drawn from the literature being criticized. If review systematically blunts that criticism, the published record understates what the field found, and the preprint is the only place the original claim survives.
This is measurable because meta-research increasingly appears as a preprint first, and both versions persist.

title: Do meta-research conclusions soften between preprint and journal?
text:
2. Hypothesis
The conclusion of a meta-research article is less critical of the practice it studied in the published version than in the preprint.

What would falsify the hypothesis. No net shift, or a shift toward more criticism. Either is publishable and the second would be the more interesting.

title: Do meta-research conclusions soften between preprint and journal?
text:
5. Exposure and outcome
There is no exposure; the contrast is version. The outcome is the direction and strength of the concluding claim, extracted from the abstract conclusion and the discussion of each version and scored on a five-point scale from strongly critical to endorsing.
Scoring is by the same gated procedure as P03: the author labels a reference sample, two models label it blind, and the study does not proceed unless a model reaches kappa 0.70 against the author.
The scorer must be blind to version. The two texts are presented in random order with dates, venue and version labels stripped, because a scorer who knows which text is the preprint knows which direction the hypothesis predicts.

title: Do meta-research conclusions soften between preprint and journal?
text:
6. Analysis, in the reduced form
The five-point ordinal outcome is not used. At 141 pairs it would spread the sample across five levels and two directions. The outcome is binary: did the concluding claim become less critical, yes or no, with unchanged pairs retained as “no”.
# McNemar on the paired binary shift. No covariates, no subgroups: at this sample
# size every added term is a term the data cannot support.
mcnemar.test(table(d$preprint_critical, d$published_critical))
Reported alongside: the raw 2x2 table, an exact binomial test on the discordant pairs, and the count of pairs by preprint server so a reader can see the arXiv concentration for themselves.
Had the probes returned 200 or more pairs, section 6 would have specified clmm(score ~ version + (1 | article)) on the ordinal score. It did not, so it does not.

text: This is an agenda item and not a proposal. It states a gap that is measured and real, and then says why the study it implies cannot be run from public data. It is published so that the gap is on the record rather than quietly skipped because it is inconvenient.

title: The field is observational about itself
section: Why this matters rather than merely being true
text:
Why this matters rather than merely being true
Meta-research grades other fields on their evidence hierarchy. It tells clinical researchers that an observational association is weaker than a randomized comparison, and it is right. Its own output is almost entirely observational association.
Some of that is unavoidable. You cannot randomize whether a paper was preregistered. But the questions the field most wants answered are causal and several of them are randomizable: whether a reporting checklist at submission improves reporting, whether blinding reviewers changes what gets accepted, whether a data availability mandate produces available data or only statements. Each of those is an intervention on a process someone controls.

title: The field is observational about itself
section: Why it cannot be run here
text:
Why it cannot be run here
Every such experiment requires randomizing something inside a journal, a funder or an ethics committee: which manuscripts get an intervention, which reviewers see what, which applicants receive which instruction. None of that is reachable from public data, and no amount of harvesting substitutes for the permission.
The honest statement is that this project can measure the gap and cannot fill it. Recording that is more useful than inventing an observational proxy and calling it an answer, which is precisely the substitution the field is criticized for elsewhere.

title: The field is observational about itself
text:
What would make it runnable
A partner willing to randomize one thing: a journal, a preprint server, a funder, or a conference with a submission process. The design is not the obstacle and would be short. The access is the obstacle.

title: The field is observational about itself
section: The one caveat on the measurement
text:
The one caveat on the measurement
Publication type is assigned by NLM indexing and an experiment can be missed. 515 of the corpus records carry no MeSH indexing at all, mostly the most recent, and an unindexed experiment would not appear in the count above. The number is a floor, not a point estimate, and the floor is four.

title: Does meta-research cite retracted work?
text:
1. The question
Citing a retracted paper as though it still stands is a documented failure of the literature, and meta-research is the field that documents it. Retracted randomized trials have been shown to go on being cited uncorrected in systematic reviews and clinical guidelines (PMID 35779825), and guidelines for low back pain have been shown to cite retracted and predatory work (PMID 40156953).
Nobody has turned that instrument on meta-research itself. A field with domain expertise in this exact failure, failing at the same rate as everyone else, would say something about how far knowing a problem gets you toward avoiding it.

title: Does meta-research cite retracted work?
text:
2. Hypothesis
Meta-research articles cite retracted work, after retraction, at a lower rate than a matched comparison of articles in the same journals and years.
Primary null. The rate ratio is 1.
What would falsify it. A rate ratio at or above 1. The direction is stated because the alternative is the interesting one.
Prior expectation. Nothing in the corpus estimates this, so the design has no anchor and does not pretend to one.

title: Does meta-research cite retracted work?
text:
3. Design
Cross-sectional study of reference lists. The unit of analysis is one reference; the unit of modeling is one article, with its matchable reference count as the offset.

title: Does meta-research cite retracted work?
text:
4. Sample
The same frame as P01v2: the qualified tier B blocks with every tier A PMID removed, screened to meta-research, restricted to PMC full text. Reusing it rather than building a third population means one screening effort, one independence argument, and one set of exclusions.
Exposed arm: screened meta-research articles. Comparison arm: articles from the same journals and years that screening excluded, which is to say articles that are not meta-research. This is a better comparison than a fresh PubMed sample because it is drawn from the same query frame and differs on exactly the axis of interest.
Both arms require a reference list in PMC. Probe PA found 4948 of the cached articles carry one.

A cited DOI counts as a citation of retracted work when it appears in OriginalPaperDOI.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Proposed by Claude Opus 5 on 2026-09-16. This protocol was published before the analysis ran and has not been edited since, apart from this note and the status field.
The study has been run. The result is at R01. Neither has been reviewed; review waits for the second reviewer’s quota on 2026-09-20.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
The question
Meta-research tells other fields to share their data. It is a field defined by holding other research to a standard. The question is whether the papers doing that holding meet the standard themselves, and more precisely whether the ones arguing hardest for it are the ones most likely to meet it.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Hypothesis
A meta-research article whose own subject is data sharing, code sharing or research transparency carries a data availability statement, and a substantive one, more often than a meta-research article on any other subject.
The hypothesis is directional and it is the interesting direction. The null is that subject matter has no relationship with practice, which would mean advocacy and behavior are independent inside the one field where they should not be.
What would falsify it. An odds ratio whose confidence interval includes or falls below 1 for the transparency-topic coefficient, with the sample large enough to exclude an effect worth caring about. That result is publishable and would be the more striking of the two.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Unit of analysis
One meta-research article. 1088 of the 1830 records in the corpus carry a PMCID and therefore have retrievable full text. The remaining 742 are excluded and the exclusion is reported, because open-access availability is itself correlated with transparency practice and this biases the sample toward the transparent. That bias works against the null and has to be stated as a limitation rather than adjusted away.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Exposure and outcome
Exposure. The datashare topic label already derived for every record in build/lit/describe.py, which matches data sharing, code availability, FAIR and data reuse vocabulary against title, abstract and keywords. 84 records carry it.
Outcome. Presence and content of a data availability statement in the full text, taken from the JATS <sec sec-type="data-availability"> element. A pilot on three records found the element present in all three, so the extraction is not hypothetical. Statements are then graded on a three-level scale, because “data are available on request” and a repository accession are not the same claim:







level
meaning




none
no statement


declarative
a statement that shares nothing: on request, within the article, not applicable


actionable
a repository name, accession, DOI or URL that resolves



Grading the middle and top levels is done by rule on the statement text, and a random 100 statements are graded by hand to measure where the rule disagrees. The rule is not adjusted after seeing the outcome.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Analysis
In R. Logistic regression of an actionable statement on the transparency topic label, adjusted for publication year, journal and article type, with journal as a random effect because a journal’s own policy is the dominant driver of whether any statement appears at all and a fixed effect on 400 journals will not estimate.
glmer(actionable ~ topic_datashare + year_c + pubtype +
        (1 | journal), family = binomial, data = d)
An ordinal model on the three-level outcome is fitted alongside as the preregistered secondary, not as a fallback if the binary result disappoints.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Novelty
This is not a transparency-of-X study with X swapped, and the distinction is the reason the proposal exists. Sofi-Mahmudi and colleagues measured the transparency of COVID-19 research (PMID 37494359) and the FAIRness of its data (PMID 39556553); both estimate a rate in a population. A 2026 study measured data availability statements in dentistry journals (PMID 41955959) and is again a rate.
This asks whether one measurable property of a paper predicts another property of the same paper. It has an exposure, an outcome and a direction, and it can come out the other way.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
What it costs
1088 PMC full-text fetches at the NCBI throttle, roughly twelve minutes, cached. The corpus is already harvested. No paid service and no API key.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Known threats to the result

Journal policy confounds everything. A journal that mandates a statement produces one regardless of the author’s convictions. The random effect absorbs the average journal, not an interaction between journal policy and topic, and the estimate is within-journal only where a journal publishes both kinds of paper.
The exposure is a vocabulary match, not a judgment. A paper labelled datashare may mention data sharing once in passing. Misclassification here is non-differential with respect to the outcome and biases toward the null, which weakens a positive finding and strengthens a negative one.
60 percent PMC coverage is not random. Stated above; not fixable within this design.

text: This project studies transparency in research. It would be indefensible for the project itself to be opaque, so every query, every count and every scope decision is recorded here, including the ones that went wrong.

title: How this was done

Databases and dates
PubMed and PMC, through the NCBI E-utilities. PMC is searched as well as PubMed because PMC carries records PubMed does not index: author manuscripts, some non-MEDLINE journals, and deposited preprints. Searches were run on 2026-09-16. No language, date or article-type limit was applied.
The harvester is build/lit/search.py. It is the only route by which a record enters the corpus, and it writes a machine-readable log of every query it issued to data/lit/search-log.json.

title: How this was done
text:
The two tiers
The field can be searched two ways and they retrieve different things.
Tier A is the field naming itself: a paper that describes its own work as meta-research, metascience, research on research, or a meta-epidemiological study. Precision is close to total, because no other kind of paper uses those words about itself.
Tier B is the field by subject matter: reporting quality, data sharing, retraction, registration, peer review, and the rest. Tier B retrieves two populations that no boolean query separates. A search for "data sharing" returns surveys of how often trials share data alongside trials that happened to share theirs, and only the first kind is meta-research.
Only tier A has been harvested. Tier B has been sized and the counts are published below, but nothing from it is in the corpus. That decision is revisited once the tier A map has been read.

The 189588
The reg block first returned 189588 records, five sixths of everything tier B retrieved, from the single phrase "trial registration". The obvious explanation was wrong. The phrase was not being broken into words and ANDed by PubMed; it is phrase-indexed, and the quoted form returns fewer records than trial AND registration does. The real cause is that Trial registration is the label of a section in a structured abstract, so every registered trial in PubMed carries the phrase verbatim. It identifies trials that were registered and never studies of registration.
The phrase has been removed from the block. build/lit/search.py records why, next to the block it was removed from, so it is not reintroduced by someone who only sees that the block looks thin.
"registered report" was removed for a related reason: the singular returns 5806 records and the plural 192, because the singular also matches any sentence about a report that was registered. Only the plural is kept.


The qualifier
For the contaminated blocks, ANDing the topic with a set of phrases that name the object of study separates a study of the literature from a study of patients. A study of data sharing examines published articles; a trial that shared its data examines people.
"published articles"  "published studies"    "published trials"
"journal articles"    "publications"         "sample of articles"
"cross-sectional study of"                   "sample of trials"
"we searched PubMed"  "we searched MEDLINE"  "we searched Embase"
"research articles"   "abstracts of"         "meta-epidemiological"
It is effective and it is lossy. A meta-research paper that describes its sample as “we examined 300 trials” carries none of these phrases and would be lost. Both numbers are therefore recorded, so any qualified corpus is reported against the raw count it was drawn from rather than presented as the whole field.

title: How this was done
section: Retrieval limits, and why nothing was silently truncated
text:
Retrieval limits, and why nothing was silently truncated
NCBI returns at most 9999 identifiers for one query. The sibling project this harvester is adapted from partitions an oversized query by year and then by month and stops there, so a single month above the ceiling truncates without saying so. Meta-research blocks are large and concentrated in recent years, which is where that would happen.
The partitioner here bisects the publication-date range recursively until every part is under the ceiling. When even a single day exceeds it, the day is recorded in gaps in the search log and printed as TRUNCATED, rather than passed off as complete. The tier A harvest needed no partitioning: both queries were under the ceiling.

title: How this was done
text:
Labelling
Topic labels are assigned in build/lit/describe.py by matching the tier B phrase vocabulary against each record’s title, abstract and author keywords. Matching is case-insensitive, treats a hyphen and a space as equivalent, as PubMed does, and requires whole-token boundaries so that spin does not match spinal.
Two vocabularies are involved and conflating them caused the one error this project has so far published. The search vocabulary is tuned for precision against all of PubMed, where a phrase as broad as "peer review" retrieves every paper that mentions having been peer reviewed. The labelling vocabulary applies inside a corpus that is already meta-research, where that same narrowness only hides topics: the search phrases labelled peer review on 11 records while 159 of them mention it, and generative AI on 1 while 66 mention a language model. A conclusion drawn from those counts, that the field does not study its own quality control, was published on the landscape page and was false.
Broad labelling phrases now live in LABEL_EXTRA in build/lit/describe.py, applied only to records already retrieved and never to a query. The corrected counts are on the landscape, which also states what the earlier version claimed.
A label means the record uses a topic’s vocabulary. It does not mean a human, or a model, judged the record to be about that topic. No model has read any record in this corpus. Records can carry several labels; 1819 of 1830 carry at least one and 11 carry none.

title: How this was done
text:
What this corpus is not

It is not the meta-research literature. It is the part of it that names itself. Work published before roughly 2015, when the vocabulary settled, largely does not appear even when it is unmistakably meta-research by subject.
It is not screened. Every record retrieved by the tier A query is in, including editorials, comments and letters. Publication types are reported on the landscape page so a reader can see how much of the corpus that is.
It carries no preprints beyond what PMC deposits. Europe PMC indexes preprint servers under a source PubMed has no equivalent for. Adding that supplement is a known gap, not an oversight.
Nothing here has been peer reviewed yet. The review process is described in the pipeline and has not run.

title: Automated meta-research
text:
Meta-research is the study of research itself: how transparently it is reported, whether its data can be found and reused, whether its results survive replication, what happens to it when it is retracted. This project asks whether that work can be done end to end by language models, under conditions strict enough that the result is worth reading.
Nothing is hidden. The search that found the literature, the map derived from it, the studies proposed against that map, the code that runs them, the reviews written by independent models, and the disagreements between those reviews are all published here, in the order they happened.

title: Automated meta-research
text:
The pipeline
1. Search. PubMed and PMC, through a harvester that logs every query it issues and cannot truncate a result set without saying so. The protocol, including the queries that turned out to be wrong and why, is in how this was done.
2. Map. Every record is labelled by vocabulary match against a topic list, and the counts are derived by a script rather than read by a model. This is deliberately the dumbest possible method: a claim on the landscape can be checked by rerunning one file.
3. Propose. Studies are proposed against the map, and a proposal has to say what is already known, which records establish it, and what specifically would be new. A proposal that cannot name the work it would extend does not get written up.
4. Run. Analyses are written and executed in R. Each study carries its data, its code and its output in the repository, so a reader can rerun it rather than trust it.
5. Review. Each study is reviewed independently by models from different providers, given the study and instructed to refute it. Reviews are published whole, including the ones that find nothing and the ones that disagree with each other. Where reviewers disagree, the disagreement is shown rather than resolved silently.

title: Automated meta-research
section: What the models did and did not do
text:
What the models did and did not do
The searching, the analysis code, the drafting and the reviewing are done by language models. The research questions, the scope decisions, the judgment about what is worth publishing, and the responsibility for everything on this site are the author’s. Where a model produced something, the page says which model and when.
This distinction matters more here than in most projects, because the subject is research quality. A site about transparency that was vague about its own provenance would be evidence against its own argument.

text:
Each proposal below is a protocol. It states a hypothesis, what would falsify it, the unit of analysis, the data source with a call that proved the source reachable, and the analysis in R, and it is published in that state before any analysis is run.
The order matters and it is deliberate. A protocol written after the result is known is not a protocol, and a project that criticizes selective reporting cannot itself decide what its question was once it has seen the answer. Every proposal therefore carries a date and a status, and a result page will link back to the protocol as it stood.

A document that asserts its sample size, its power or its feasibility rather than measuring them is a design, whatever it calls itself.

text:
Review
Nothing here has been reviewed. Review is by two models from different providers, each given the document and instructed to refute it, with output validated against a schema and adjudicated by the fixed rule in build/audit/adjudicate.py. That rule downgrades an unsubstantiated severe finding rather than counting it, lets a lone reviewer holding a verbatim quote block a document two others called sound, and publishes a contested document as contested rather than picking a winner. Twelve golden cases pin it.
No document is reviewed by one model alone. The Codex account’s usage limit was exhausted on 2026-09-16 and resets on 2026-09-20, so reviews begin then.
The five documents at protocol stage go first. The three designs are reviewed when their probes complete, because a reviewer asked to assess feasibility numbers that do not exist yet is being asked to review a wish.

title: The agenda
text:
How these were chosen
The selection rule was to turn the field’s own instrument on the field. Meta-research measures whether others share data, cite retracted work, follow checklists, replicate, and report inconvenient findings. Those questions had not been asked about meta-research itself, and most are answerable from data already harvested or openly available.
The rule also kept out the obvious alternative. A study measuring transparency, or FAIRness, in one more specialty is a rate in a new population, and rates in new populations are what this corpus already holds in quantity. Every document here has an exposure, an outcome and a direction, and every one can come out the other way.
One candidate was dropped for lack of novelty rather than lack of interest: a study relating a journal’s transparency policy score to the transparency of the meta-research it publishes. The corpus search found PMID 37433624, a systematic review with individual participant data meta-analysis of predictors of data and code sharing, which covers it. It is recorded here because a dropped idea and the reason it was dropped are part of the trail.
P04 is not runnable and says so. P09 is the most important question of the set and is the least far along, which is a fact about difficulty rather than about priority.

Defects are part of the result
Every study here reports the bugs found during its own run, what each one cost, and which direction the correction moved the estimate. That is not modesty. Generated analysis code fails silently: it produces a number rather than an error, and the number is plausible. The first study found two such defects, one of which was inflating its own effect through an artifact and one of which was suppressing it.
A result published without that section is a result whose checks either were not run or were not reported, and neither is a reason to trust it more.

title: Advocacy and practice in meta-research: protocol
text:
1. Why this design exists
R01 found that meta-research articles about data sharing point at a repository of their own about four times as often as meta-research articles on other subjects. That result is exploratory and cannot be made confirmatory after the fact, for three reasons stated on its own page: the grading rule was developed by reading the analysis data, three of four sensitivity analyses were post hoc, and no human validation was done.
This specifies a confirmatory test of the same hypothesis, on a sample R01 did not use, with every instrument fixed before any data are retrieved.

title: Advocacy and practice in meta-research: protocol
text:
2. Objective and hypothesis
Primary objective. To test whether a meta-research article whose subject is data sharing, code availability or research transparency is more likely than a meta-research article on another aspect of research practice to carry an actionable data availability statement of its own.
Primary hypothesis. It is, and the association is directional.
Primary null. The odds ratio for the transparency exposure is 1.
What would falsify the hypothesis. An adjusted odds ratio whose 95 percent confidence interval includes 1, in a sample powered as in section 7. Section 7 fixes the power in advance so that a null can be read as evidence of absence rather than absence of evidence, which was not true of R01.
Prior expectation, stated so it cannot be revised. R01 estimated 4.40 (1.80 to 10.75) on a different sample with a rule developed on that sample. Regression to the mean and the removal of rule-development bias both predict a smaller effect here. An estimate between 1.5 and 3 would be consistent with R01; an estimate at or above 4 would be surprising and should itself be treated with suspicion rather than as confirmation.

4.2 Eligibility
Include an article when all of the following hold:

Retrieved by the qualified tier B search for one of the four blocks above.
Not present in the tier A corpus harvested on 2026-09-16.
Screened as meta-research: its object of study is published research, researchers, journals or the research process, rather than patients, organisms, materials or clinical outcomes.
Present in PMC with a <body> element longer than 500 characters, so that a statement could have been extracted had one existed.

Exclude an article when any of the following hold:

Its publication type is comment, editorial, letter, news, biography or historical article. R01 estimated an odds ratio of 0.04 for this group; an article with no data of its own belongs to a different population and its absence of a statement is not evidence about sharing behavior. R01 adjusted for this. This protocol excludes it, which is cleaner.
It is a retracted publication or a retraction notice.
It is not in English. R01 applied no language limit; a statement in another language would be graded none by an English-language rule, which is a measurement failure rather than a finding.



4.3 Screening
Criterion 3 is the one no boolean query settles, and the reason tier B was never harvested for the map. Screening is on title and abstract, by two models from different providers, each given the same written criterion and blind to the other.

Both agree include: included.
Both agree exclude: excluded.
Disagreement: adjudicated by the author. The count of disagreements is reported.

Before screening the frame, 200 records sampled at random across the four blocks are screened by the author to create a reference standard. Agreement is reported as Cohen’s kappa per model. If neither model reaches kappa 0.75 against the reference standard, screening by model is abandoned and the study proceeds on a random subsample screened entirely by the author, with the sample size reduced accordingly and the power recomputed and reported.

title: Advocacy and practice in meta-research: protocol
text:
5. Exposure
Exposed: retrieved by the qualified datashare block and screened in.
Unexposed: retrieved by the qualified report, reg or repro blocks, screened in, and not also retrieved by the datashare block.
An article retrieved by datashare and by another block is exposed. The exposure is whether transparency is among the article’s subjects, not whether it is the only one.
This is a coarser exposure than a judgment of what an article is primarily about, and that is deliberate: it is reproducible from a query string, and its misclassification is toward the null. The alternative, asking a model what each article is mainly about, adds a second instrument needing its own validation to measure something the query already approximates.

6. Outcome

6.1 Extraction
The data availability statement is taken from the JATS full text by studies/P01-advocacy-and-practice/extract.py as it stands at commit 158164be700a596610a074533e6509ce142a6774, unchanged. A prose pin is not a pin; that hash is the pin, and git show 158164be700a596610a074533e6509ce142a6774:studies/P01-advocacy-and-practice/extract.py is how a reader checks it. That code searches <front> and <back> only, never <body>, in this order: a section or notes block with a sec-type or notes-type naming data availability; a section or notes block whose title matches the data availability pattern; a custom-meta pair whose name matches it.
The restriction to front and back matter is not a detail. Without it, a paper about data availability has its own methods and results read as its disclosure, which is the artifact that contaminated 4 of 43 exposed records in R01 and is documented there.


6.2 Grading
Three ordered levels, graded by the rule in studies/_shared/R/grade.R at that same commit, reproduced here in full so that no later edit can pass unnoticed:







grade
definition




none
no statement in front or back matter


declarative
a statement that shares nothing: available on request, contained within the article or its supplementary files, or not applicable


actionable
a named repository, or a DOI or URL that is not the article’s own



Tests apply in this order, and the order is itself pre-specified because changing it changes the result:

A named repository present, from the fixed list in REPO: actionable. A repository outranks a co-occurring on-request clause, because an article that deposits its code and separately withholds licensed raw data has shared what it could.
An on-request clause present: declarative.
A not-applicable clause present: declarative.
A DOI or URL present that is not the article’s own DOI: actionable.
Otherwise: declarative.

Primary outcome: actionable versus not.
Secondary outcome: the three-level ordinal grade.


6.3 Validation of the grading rule
This is a gate, not a report. 150 statements, stratified by rule grade, are graded by the author, blind to the article’s exposure and to the rule’s grade. Agreement is reported as Cohen’s kappa with a 95 percent confidence interval.

Kappa at or above 0.80: the rule is used as the primary instrument.
Kappa 0.60 to 0.79: the rule is used, and the primary analysis is repeated on the hand-graded subsample alone as a co-primary, with both reported together regardless of whether they agree.
Kappa below 0.60: the rule is abandoned. The study proceeds on a hand-graded random sample, with power recomputed and reported.

The rule is not modified after seeing the validation. If validation shows it is wrong, the wrongness is reported and the fallback above is taken. This is the commitment R01 could not make because its rule was written while the data were being read.

section: 12. What this design still cannot do
text:
12. What this design still cannot do

It is not causal. Researchers who study transparency and researchers who practice it may be the same people, and the design cannot separate selection from influence.
PMC coverage is not random. Open-access availability correlates with transparency practice, so both arms lean transparent. The direction of bias on a comparison between arms is not obvious and is not claimed to be toward the null.
The qualified frame is lossy. The study-of-literature qualifier cut the raw datashare block from 15418 to 754, and a meta-research paper describing its sample as “we examined 300 trials” carries none of the qualifier phrases and is absent from the frame. The sample is a high-precision slice of the field, not the field.
It tests association in one direction only. A finding that transparency-topic papers share more does not tell us whether writing about transparency changes behavior or whether people who already share choose to write about it.

title: Is bad news cited more?
text:
1. The question
Meta-research reports on how well other research is done, and the answer is usually that it is done badly. If findings of failure are rewarded with citations more than findings that a practice is adequate, the field faces an incentive gradient pointing at one conclusion, and that gradient would be invisible within any single study.
This is publication bias asked about the field that studies publication bias, and asked at the citation stage rather than at acceptance.

Among meta-research articles, those concluding that the practice studied is inadequate accrue more citations than those concluding it is adequate, adjusted for age, journal and topic.

A stratified random sample of 300 abstracts is classified by the author into inadequate, adequate, mixed, or not applicable. This is the reference standard. A model does not produce it, for the reason R01 already demonstrated: a model checking a rule another model wrote found a real defect and still left agreement with a person unknown.

Agreement is reported as Cohen’s kappa against the reference standard and between models.
If neither model reaches kappa 0.70 against the author’s labels, the study stops and the negative methodological result is published. Whether a language model can read the direction of a scientific conclusion is itself worth knowing.
Only above the threshold does classification extend to the rest, with the measured misclassification rate carried into a sensitivity analysis.

title: When two meta-research studies measure the same thing, do they agree?
text:
ImportantStatus: design. The pair-counting probe has not run. Not a protocol.



This is the strongest novelty claim of the set and the weakest on feasibility. Section 2 records the searches that establish the first; probe PA decides the second.

title: When two meta-research studies measure the same thing, do they agree?
text:
1. The question
Meta-research tells other fields that a finding which does not replicate is not a finding. The field publishes many studies measuring the same practices: reporting quality in a specialty, data sharing in a set of journals, registration adherence in a trial population. Their samples overlap. Nobody has asked whether they agree.
If two meta-research studies measuring the same practice over overlapping literature report materially different rates, the field’s own evidence base has the property it criticizes elsewhere.

title: When two meta-research studies measure the same thing, do they agree?
section: 2. Novelty, with the searches that establish it
text:
2. Novelty, with the searches that establish it
Claims of novelty in this project must show the search that produced them, because a model-recalled absence of prior work is not evidence of absence.
Corpus regex, over 1830 tier A records and 7412 frame records, title and abstract:
(concordan|discordan|agreement|consisten).{0,50}between.{0,40}
(methodological review|meta-research|cross-sectional stud).{0,40}(same|identical)
|overlapping (methodological|meta-research)
Result: 0 records.
What does exist, and is the closest prior work, is PMID 37433624, a systematic review with individual participant data meta-analysis of studies investigating data and code sharing. It pools meta-research studies; it does not ask whether they agree with each other. That distinction is the study.
This section is updated, not deleted, if review finds prior work the searches missed.

title: When two meta-research studies measure the same thing, do they agree?
text:
3. Hypothesis
Pairs of meta-research studies measuring the same practice in overlapping populations report rates that differ by more than sampling error alone would produce.
Primary null. Between-study heterogeneity in the paired rate difference is consistent with sampling variation.
What would falsify it. Heterogeneity consistent with chance, which would be a strong positive result about the field and is the outcome the field would hope for.

title: When two meta-research studies measure the same thing, do they agree?
text:
4. Sample
The unit is a pair, and pairs are what the probe must count before anything else is decided. Candidate pairs come from two places:

The included-study lists of meta-research syntheses already in the corpus. PMID 37433624 is the largest and its included studies are, by construction, meta-research studies measuring the same construct.
The corpus itself, matched on topic block plus the population studied, extracted from the abstract.

A pair qualifies when both studies measure the same practice, in the same discipline or journal set, over overlapping publication years, and both report an extractable rate with a denominator.

title: When two meta-research studies measure the same thing, do they agree?
text:
5. Outcome
The absolute difference in reported rate between the two members of a pair, with each study’s own denominator, so that the expected difference under sampling variation alone is computable.

title: When two meta-research studies measure the same thing, do they agree?
text:
6. Analysis
In R. For each pair, the observed rate difference against the difference expected from the two binomial denominators. Aggregated as an excess-heterogeneity statistic across pairs, with a permutation null built by pairing studies that do not share a population.
The permutation null is the part that makes this a test rather than a description: without it, any two rates differ and the result is unfalsifiable.

title: Does meta-research change the practice it documents?
text:
ImportantStatus: design only. No probe has run. This is the one that most needs the author’s judgment.



Every other document here can have its feasibility settled by a script. This one cannot, because its unit of analysis is “a documented problem” and enumerating those is a judgment about which meta-research papers were consequential enough to have plausibly changed anything.
Published at design stage deliberately. It is the most important question in the set and pretending otherwise by deferring it would be a choice about what is easy rather than what matters.

title: Does meta-research change the practice it documents?
text:
1. The question
Meta-research documents problems on the assumption that documenting them helps. That assumption is rarely tested, and the field that insists on evidence for other people’s interventions has little for its own.

title: Does meta-research change the practice it documents?
text:
2. Hypothesis
Publication of a meta-research study documenting poor practice in a defined population is followed by improvement in that practice, beyond the secular trend.
Primary null. No change in level or slope at the publication date, beyond trend.
What would falsify it. No discontinuity and no slope change. Given how many such studies exist and how little practice appears to move, the null is the more likely outcome and the design must be able to report it credibly. That is why it is an interrupted time series with a control series rather than a before-and-after comparison.

title: Does meta-research change the practice it documents?
text:
3. Design
Controlled interrupted time series. For each documented problem:

Intervention: publication of the meta-research study.
Series: the practice it measured, re-measured by us at regular intervals before and after, in the same population the study defined.
Control series: the same practice over the same period in a comparable population the study did not examine.

The control series is what separates a real effect from the secular improvement that affects everything. A study reporting improvement without one is measuring the calendar.

title: Does meta-research change the practice it documents?
section: 4. Sample, and what the author must decide
text:
4. Sample, and what the author must decide
The unit is a documented problem. A candidate qualifies when the original study:

defines its population explicitly enough to reconstruct it from a query,
reports a rate with a denominator,
was published at least three years ago, so there is post-period to observe,
measures something re-measurable from metadata or full text without human reading at scale.

Criterion 4 is the binding one. “Adherence to CONSORT item 6a” is not re-measurable at scale; “carries a data availability statement”, “reports a registration number”, “is registered prospectively” are.
The author selects the candidate problems. A model proposing which papers were influential would be choosing the intervention to suit the hypothesis, and there is no defensible automatic criterion. Five to ten problems is the target.

title: Does meta-research change the practice it documents?
text:
5. Analysis
In R. Segmented regression per problem, with a control series and autocorrelation handled explicitly.
gls(rate ~ time + level + trend + series + series:level + series:trend,
    correlation = corARMA(p = 1), data = d)
Pooled across problems by random-effects meta-analysis of the level and slope changes, since a single problem is a case study and the question is about the field.

What this cannot show

It cannot attribute change to the paper rather than to the concern that produced the paper. This is the central limitation and no observational design removes it.

A null result would not show that meta-research is useless, only that this particular route from documentation to practice is not visible at this resolution.
